dedupe_keys.name: community led coastal restoration on the maharees peninsula ireland

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes how the Maharees Conservation Association, founded by the local community in 2016, restores the dunes of the Maharees, a 5 km sandy tombolo on the Dingle peninsula in County Kerry, Ireland, which is exposed to storms, erosion, sea level rise and heavy tourism. Members from hospitality, tourism, farming and education, with councils, national agencies, NGOs and researchers, have carried out nature-based measures such as sand-trapping fences (20 volunteers built a 1 km fence in three days) and marram grass planting to rebuild dunes that protect the road and settlements. Funding came mainly from Kerry County Council and the National Parks and Wildlife Service, with many smaller grants, and volunteer work kept costs low. Projections cited include wetter autumns and winters and drier summers under SSP5-8.5. The page, published in October 2025 and updated in September 2026, is accessible online as free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal with links to research reports and the association's website. Caveats: costs and dune growth are not quantified, and the approach relies on sustained volunteer effort. It illustrates community-led nature-based coastal hazard reduction and climate adaptation; related records are the Hesketh Out Marsh and Sand Motor case studies and WDPA.
name: Community-led coastal restoration on the Maharees peninsula, Ireland
notes: That the dunes protect the road and settlements is inferred from the page's description of the tombolo; the page read did not state which assets are protected.
outcomes: Since 2016 the community partnership has built dune fences and replanted marram grass, strengthening the tombolo's dunes at low cost through volunteers and diverse funding.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study based on EPA Ireland research and Maharees Conservation Association sources
